page: Amazon Web Services c9g.large is a compute-optimized server instance powered by the AWS Graviton processor family. It features 2 dedicated physical cores on the ARMv9 arm64 architecture, running at 3.3 GHz with a Neoverse-V3 model design. The CPU includes 64 KB L1d cache, 2 MB L2 cache, and 48 MB L3 cache. It is equipped with 4.0 GB of system memory, providing a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 2.0 GB per core. This instance operates on the Nitro hypervisor, lacks local storage, and has a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. No GPUs are included.

Performance benchmarks reveal strong single-core capabilities but limited multi-core scaling due to the 2-core configuration. The instance achieves top-tier results in single-threaded operations, including a Geekbench single-core score of 2306.0, single-threaded gzip compression at 36.49 GB/sec, and single-threaded bzip3 decompression at 17.21 GB/sec. Conversely, multi-core and multi-threaded benchmarks, such as Geekbench multi-core (4174.0) and stress-ng multi-core (4001.26), fall into the lower performance tiers. Memory performance is mixed, with average read bandwidth on large blocks (64.7 GB/sec) but weaker write bandwidth (24.76 GB/sec) and poor encryption performance.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the c9g.large offers a modern ARMv9 architecture with dedicated cores at a low resource density, making it a viable option for single-threaded tasks or lightweight workloads that do not require high memory capacity or local storage. It is well-suited for single-threaded data processing, basic web serving, text processing, and lightweight database operations. It is less suitable for multi-threaded compilation, heavy cryptography, or memory-intensive applications.

It features 2 dedicated physical cores, 4.0 GB of memory, and operates on the Nitro hypervisor with a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps and no local storage. Benchmarks indicate exceptional single-core performance, with top-tier results in single-threaded gzip compression, bzip3 decompression, and Geekbench single-core tests. However, its multi-core scaling and memory write bandwidth are relatively weak due to its 2-core limitation. This instance is highly efficient for single-threaded processing, lightweight web serving, and text processing workloads, but is less suited for multi-threaded compilation or memory-heavy tasks.
